summary: Defines a Content-ID access method for the MIME Message/External-Body type, letting an external body refer to an object by the Content-ID of another part of the message. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: The content-id access type lets one MIME part point to another part in the same message. A mail reader combines the reference with the original content, so the message can include repeated data only once.

questions: what is the content-id access type
how does message/external-body refer to objects
how can a mime part refer to another part
how does content-id avoid duplicate data
subtitle: A MIME body part can refer to another part in the same message by Content-ID.

tldr.problem: A structured object in a MIME message can reuse the same data in several places, which would otherwise require sending duplicate body parts.
tldr.mechanism: A Message/External-Body part uses access-type content-id and a Content-ID that matches exactly one other part in the same multipart message.
tldr.outcome: A mail user agent constructs a complete part from the referring part's headers and the referenced part's content. The RFC is Experimental.

today: RFC 1873 defines an Experimental MIME access type. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Avoiding Duplicate Message Data
sections.content:
A multipart MIME message can represent a structured object whose elements map to separate body parts. If several elements contain the same data, sending that data repeatedly uses extra bandwidth and storage.

RFC 1873 defines an access type that lets one body part refer to another within the same message. This keeps the object's structure while including the repeated data only once.
sections.plainLanguage: When multiple parts need the same content, a message can send the content once and let other parts refer to it. This avoids copying the same data into each part.

sections.title: How a Content-ID Reference Works
sections.content:
The access-type name is content-id, with no required or optional parameters. Its Content-ID must be identical to the Content-ID of exactly one other part in the same message, excluding other content-id access-type entities. Therefore, it can be used only inside a multipart message.

The mail user agent builds the result using the referenced part's Content-Type and body, the referring part's other headers, any additional headers from the referenced part, and the separating blank line.
sections.plainLanguage: The reference uses a Content-ID that matches one other part in the same message. The mail reader combines that part's content with the headers supplied by the referring part.

sections.title: An Example with Repeated Images
sections.content:
The RFC's example contains a JPEG image with a Content-ID, followed by a Message/External-Body part whose access type is content-id and whose Content-ID matches the image. The second part has no separate image body.

The mail user agent can construct the second image part with the referenced image's content and the second part's Content-Description header. The example uses this to represent an image duplicated by reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The message contains an image once and then includes a reference with the same Content-ID. The mail reader uses the original image content for the referenced part.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says this access type does not affect the security of messages or systems. It also notes that the MIME entity being referenced may have security implications of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The reference itself does not change message security. The content it points to may still have security implications.

references.text: Crocker, D., "Standard for the Format of ARPA Internet Text Messages", STD 11, RFC 822, UDEL, August 1982.
